Young animals were preferred as their skin was soft, which made it easy to work with. [Q31]

They were constructed from specially sharpened stone, so have survived remarkably well. [Q32]

The colours themselves occurred naturally in minerals that were dug up from the ground and processed, usually by mixing with water. [Q33]

Many more guanaco were hunted after the introduction of the horse to the region, which made the Patagon people more mobile. [Q34]

Another important development was that the Spanish themselves liked, were great admirers of the coats and bought them for high prices, so that while in the past guanaco had only been hunted to meet subsistence needs, now the coats were increasingly part of a commercial process, I mean something that could be bought and sold for money. [Q35]

Most important for coat making, the old scrapers used for cleaning the skins were replaced with new ones made from glass, and this was more effective and easier to keep sharp. [Q36]

We are able to say this with some confidence because very similar designs have been found in examples of art painted on the rock walls of caves that have very ancient origins. [Q37]

One possibility is that the designs may have represented a way of connecting with ancestors from previous times, and this is certainly an idea that deserves further investigation. [Q38]

Because the natural habitat of the young Guanaco was the rich grasslands of inland areas, it seems unlikely that these were constructed around the coast, but rather in parts of the interior. [Q39]

Finally, we should note that the traditional art of coat making has long since been lost in this region, but Patagon shepherds today do still employ some of the same techniques to make blankets in the winter months, though there is no painting or design work involved. [Q40]
